title: Time Series Analysis and Forecasting
subtitle: Analyse and forecast time series in Python: decomposition, stationarity, exponential smoothing, SARIMA and gradient boosting, tested with honest backtests and prediction intervals.
outcomes: Prepare daily time series in pandas: a regular calendar, gaps filled sensibly, and known future events
Decompose a series into trend and seasonal components and measure their strength
Test for stationarity and read ACF and PACF plots to choose differencing and model orders
Fit, diagnose and compare ETS and SARIMA models with calendar regressors in statsmodels
Forecast with gradient boosting on lag and calendar features without leaking the future
Backtest forecasters from rolling origins, choose metrics that fit the decision, and check interval coverage
prerequisites: Python and pandas, as in Data Analysis with Python and pandas, and basic statistics, as in Statistics for Data Science and AI. Machine Learning Foundations with Python helps for module 4. Install Python 3.10 or later, then pip install pandas statsmodels scikit-learn matplotlib; JupyterLab is optional but used in the walkthroughs.
description:
Every organisation that holds stock, staffs a service or plans a budget forecasts something. This course teaches you to analyse a time series and forecast it well, with the methods professionals rely on and the testing that shows whether they work. You'll work with four years of daily medicine demand from a fictional rural health district, with weekly and seasonal patterns, public holidays, outreach campaigns and gaps in the reporting, the kind of data a district medical store really has to plan from.

You'll clean and decompose the series, test for stationarity and read autocorrelation, fit exponential smoothing and SARIMA models with statsmodels, and build a gradient boosting forecaster on lag and calendar features without leaking the future. Then you'll evaluate them properly: rolling-origin backtests, metrics chosen for the decision (and why MAPE so often misleads), and prediction intervals whose coverage you check. It goes well beyond the forecasting lesson in AI-Powered Business Intelligence Fundamentals and the time-based cross-validation in Feature Engineering and Model Evaluation. Every lab prints real results that your instructor checks, and the capstone produces four-week forecasts with intervals for three medicines.

modules.title: Time series data, components and baselines
modules.summary: Get a daily series into shape in pandas, see its trend and seasonal patterns with decomposition, and set the baselines that every forecast has to beat.

lessons.title: Time series data in pandas
objectives: Index a series by time and give it a regular frequency
Find and fill gaps without inventing patterns
Resample between daily, weekly and monthly views
key_points: A time series is a sequence of measurements in time order, usually at a regular interval such as daily; in pandas it's a Series with a DatetimeIndex, for example from pd.read_csv(..., parse_dates=['date'], index_col='date').
asfreq('D') puts a series on a complete daily calendar, so days missing from an export appear as NaN instead of silently vanishing; most forecasting models assume exactly one value per period.

Tell missing values from real zeros: a day with no report is unknown, while a closed clinic really dispensed nothing; filling a gap with 0 invents a collapse in demand, and dropping zeros hides real closures.
Fill short gaps in a seasonal series from the same point in the cycle, such as the mean of the same weekday a week before and after, rather than with a straight line drawn across the weekly pattern.
resample('W').sum() or resample('MS').mean() aggregates to a coarser frequency: sum quantities and average rates, and drop partial periods at either end, which give misleading totals.

Know what the series measures: units dispensed fall when stock runs out, so on stock-out days dispensing records supply rather than demand, and those days need flagging before any model learns from them.

lessons.title: Trend, seasonality and decomposition
objectives: Describe the trend, seasonal and remainder components of a series
Choose between additive and multiplicative decomposition
Decompose a series with STL or MSTL and measure seasonal strength
key_points: A decomposition splits a series into a trend (the slowly changing level), one or more seasonal components (patterns that repeat with a fixed period, such as 7 days or a year) and a remainder, whatever is left.

Additive decomposition, y = trend + season + remainder, suits seasonal swings of constant size; when swings grow with the level, use a multiplicative one, or take logs first, since log(trend × season) = log trend + log season.

STL (Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS) estimates components with local regressions, lets the seasonal pattern change slowly and resists outliers with robust=True; MSTL extends it to several periods, such as weekly and yearly patterns in daily data.

Classical decomposition (seasonal_decompose) uses centred moving averages, so it loses values at both ends of the series and assumes the seasonal pattern never changes; prefer STL or MSTL for real data.
Seasonal strength, max(0, 1 - Var(remainder) / Var(seasonal + remainder)), runs from 0 to 1; a value near 1 means the pattern dominates the noise, and any useful forecast has to reproduce it.

lessons.title: Baselines and a first honest test
objectives: Build naive, seasonal naive, mean and drift forecasts
Hold out the most recent period to test a forecast
Explain why every model has to beat a baseline
key_points: The naive forecast repeats the last value; seasonal naive repeats the value from one season earlier, such as the same weekday last week; the mean forecast repeats the historical average; drift extends the line from the first value to the last.
Baselines cost almost nothing and set the bar: a model that can't beat seasonal naive on a strongly seasonal series isn't worth its complexity, however well it fits the training data.
Test on the future: hold out the most recent stretch, as long as the forecast horizon, fit on everything before it, and never let the test period inform the model, its features or its tuning.
The horizon comes from the decision: a store that orders every four weeks needs forecasts 1 to 28 days ahead, so measure errors over those 28 days, not just one day ahead.
One holdout is a single sample of the future and is dominated by whatever happened in it, such as holidays; backtests from several origins, in module 5, give a steadier comparison.

"""Generate the course data: four years of daily medicine demand in a fictional rural health district.

    python make_demand.py

demand.csv has one row per day from 2022-01-01 to 2025-12-31 as the district's reporting system exported it,
so some days are missing and a few values are blank:

date                 the day
holiday              1 on a public holiday, when most clinics close
campaign             1 on a day of a planned community outreach campaign (known months in advance)
ors_sachets          oral rehydration salts sachets dispensed (the series used in the labs)
paracetamol_packs    paracetamol packs dispensed
amoxicillin_courses  amoxicillin courses dispensed (small numbers, sometimes zero)

Only random.random() and basic arithmetic are used, with a fixed seed, so everyone gets the same data.
"""

import csv
import math
import random
from datetime import date, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

R, RP, RA, RM = (random.Random(seed) for seed in (7, 8, 9, 10))   # one generator per series, one for gaps
START, DAYS = date(2022, 1, 1), 1461
WEEKDAY = [1.30, 1.12, 1.05, 1.02, 0.98, 0.55, 0.20]                  # Monday to Sunday
ORS_MONTH = [1.30, 1.35, 1.20, 1.00, 0.85, 0.75, 0.72, 0.75, 0.85, 0.95, 1.10, 1.22]   # the rainy season peaks
PARA_MONTH = [0.95, 0.95, 1.00, 1.05, 1.12, 1.20, 1.22, 1.15, 1.02, 0.95, 0.92, 0.92]  # the cold season peaks
MID = [15, 45, 74, 105, 135, 166, 196, 227, 258, 288, 319, 349]       # mid-month day of the year
HOLIDAYS = [(1, 1), (3, 21), (4, 27), (5, 1), (6, 16), (8, 9), (9, 24), (12, 16), (12, 25), (12, 26)]
CAMPAIGNS = [date(2022, 3, 14), date(2022, 10, 10), date(2023, 3, 13), date(2023, 10, 9),
             date(2024, 3, 11), date(2024, 10, 7), date(2025, 3, 10), date(2025, 10, 13)]    # Mondays
OUTAGE = (date(2024, 7, 8), date(2024, 7, 12))                       # the reporting system was down


def seasonal(table, d):
    """The month factor for day d, interpolated between mid-month points, wrapping round the year."""
    doy = d.timetuple().tm_yday - 1
    for i in range(12):
        a, b = MID[i], MID[(i + 1) % 12] + (365 if i == 11 else 0)
        x = doy if doy >= MID[0] or i < 11 else doy + 365
        if a <= x < b:
            w = (x - a) / (b - a)
            return table[i] * (1 - w) + table[(i + 1) % 12] * w
    return table[0]


def normal(r):
    return sum(r.random() for _ in range(12)) - 6.0


def poisson(lam):
    limit, k, p = math.exp(-lam), 0, 1.0
    while True:
        p *= RA.random()
        if p <= limit:
            return k
        k += 1


def main():
    campaign_days = {c + timedelta(days=i) for c in CAMPAIGNS for i in range(5)}
    rows = []
    for t in range(DAYS):
        d = START + timedelta(days=t)
        holiday = int((d.month, d.day) in HOLIDAYS)
        campaign = int(d in campaign_days)
        week = WEEKDAY[d.weekday()] * (0.25 if holiday else 1.0)
        ors = (300 + 0.06 * t) * seasonal(ORS_MONTH, d) * week * (1.6 if campaign else 1.0)
        ors = max(0, round(ors * (1 + 0.08 * normal(R))))
        para = (520 + 0.05 * t) * seasonal(PARA_MONTH, d) * week
        para = max(0, round(para * (1 + 0.06 * normal(RP))))
        amox = poisson((11 + 0.002 * t) * seasonal(ORS_MONTH, d) ** 0.5 * week)
        if OUTAGE[0] <= d <= OUTAGE[1] or RM.random() < 0.015:
            continue                                    # the day never reached the export
        values = [ors, para, amox]
        if RM.random() < 0.006:
            values[0] = ""                               # a clinic's report arrived empty
        rows.append([d.isoformat(), holiday, campaign, *values])
    out = Path(__file__).with_name("demand.csv")
    with open(out, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["date", "holiday", "campaign", "ors_sachets", "paracetamol_packs", "amoxicillin_courses"])
        w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"Wrote {len(rows)} days to {out.name}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Helpers for every lab: load the district's demand export, clean a series, build the calendar, and score forecasts.

    from ts_common import load, clean_series, calendar, scores, TEST_START
"""

from datetime import date, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

HERE = Path(__file__).parent
HORIZON = 28                     # forecast four weeks ahead: the district orders stock every four weeks
TEST_START = "2025-12-04"        # the last 28 days are the holdout
HOLIDAYS = [(1, 1), (3, 21), (4, 27), (5, 1), (6, 16), (8, 9), (9, 24), (12, 16), (12, 25), (12, 26)]
CAMPAIGNS = [date(2022, 3, 14), date(2022, 10, 10), date(2023, 3, 13), date(2023, 10, 9),
             date(2024, 3, 11), date(2024, 10, 7), date(2025, 3, 10), date(2025, 10, 13)]   # five weekdays each


def load():
    """The raw export, indexed by date."""
    if not (HERE / "demand.csv").exists():
        raise SystemExit("No data yet: run python make_demand.py first.")
    return pd.read_csv(HERE / "demand.csv", parse_dates=["date"], index_col="date")


def clean_series(df, column="ors_sachets"):
    """A daily series without gaps: each missing day gets the mean of the same weekday a week before and
    a week after, and anything still missing is interpolated."""
    y = df[column].asfreq("D")
    return y.fillna((y.shift(7) + y.shift(-7)) / 2).interpolate()


def calendar(index):
    """Regressors known in advance for any dates: holiday and campaign flags, and two pairs of yearly
    Fourier terms (smooth waves with periods of one year and half a year)."""
    days = {c + timedelta(days=i) for c in CAMPAIGNS for i in range(5)}
    t = (index - pd.Timestamp("2022-01-01")).days.to_numpy()
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=index)
    out["holiday"] = [int((d.month, d.day) in HOLIDAYS) for d in index]
    out["campaign"] = [int(d.date() in days) for d in index]
    for k in (1, 2):
        out[f"sin{k}"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * k * t / 365.25)
        out[f"cos{k}"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * k * t / 365.25)
    return out


def scores(actual, forecast, train=None, m=7):
    """MAE, RMSE, MAPE (%), WAPE (%) and, given the training series, MASE against a seasonal naive forecast."""
    a, f = np.asarray(actual, float), np.asarray(forecast, float)
    e = a - f
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):          # MAPE is infinite when an actual is 0
        out = {"MAE": np.mean(np.abs(e)), "RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean(e ** 2)),
               "MAPE": 100 * np.mean(np.abs(e) / np.abs(a)), "WAPE": 100 * np.sum(np.abs(e)) / np.sum(np.abs(a))}
    if train is not None:
        tr = np.asarray(train, float)
        out["MASE"] = out["MAE"] / np.mean(np.abs(tr[m:] - tr[:-m]))
    return {k: round(float(v), 3) for k, v in out.items()}

"""Lab 1: find the gaps, fill them, decompose the series and score four baseline forecasts."""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import MSTL

from ts_common import HORIZON, TEST_START, load, scores

df = load()

# TODO 2: fill each gap with the mean of the same weekday a week before and after, then interpolate
filled = y.interpolate()

weekday = filled.groupby(filled.index.dayofweek).mean().round(1)

# Decompose log demand into a trend, a weekly and a yearly seasonal component, and a remainder
res = MSTL(np.log(filled), periods=(7, 365)).fit()
for col in res.seasonal.columns:
    s = res.seasonal[col]
    # TODO 3: the seasonal strength: max(0, 1 - Var(remainder) / Var(seasonal + remainder))
    strength = 0.0
    print(f"Strength of {col}: {strength:.3f}")
trend = np.exp(res.trend)
print(f"Trend level: {trend.iloc[0]:.1f} at the start, {trend.iloc[-1]:.1f} at the end")

train, test = filled[:pd.Timestamp(TEST_START) - pd.Timedelta(days=1)], filled[TEST_START:]
h = np.arange(1, HORIZON + 1)
baselines = {
    "naive": np.repeat(train.iloc[-1], HORIZON),
    # TODO 4: seasonal naive (the last week, repeated) and drift (the line from the first to the last value)
    "seasonal naive": np.repeat(np.nan, HORIZON),
    "mean": np.repeat(train.mean(), HORIZON),
    "drift": np.repeat(np.nan, HORIZON),
}
for name, forecast in baselines.items():
    s = scores(test, forecast)
    print(f"{name:15} MAE {s['MAE']:7.1f}  RMSE {s['RMSE']:7.1f}")

hints: y.isna().sum() counts the missing values once the series is on a daily calendar.
np.tile(a, 4) repeats an array four times: seven days repeated give 28.
Drift's slope is (last - first) / (number of values - 1).

modules.title: Stationarity and autocorrelation
modules.summary: Learn what stationarity means and why models rely on it, make a series stationary with transformations and differencing, and read autocorrelation to see what structure is left to model.

lessons.title: Stationarity, transformations and differencing
objectives: Explain stationarity and why ARIMA-type models need it
Stabilise variance with logs or Box-Cox transformations
Remove trend and seasonality by differencing, without overdoing it
key_points: A (weakly) stationary series has a constant mean, a constant variance and autocorrelations that depend only on the lag, not on when you look; trends, seasonality and variance that changes with the level all break it.

A log or Box-Cox transformation stabilises variance that grows with the level and turns multiplicative patterns additive; forecast on that scale and transform back, remembering that exp of a forecast of log demand is nearer the median than the mean.
First differencing, y_t - y_(t-1), removes a trend or a wandering level; seasonal differencing, y_t - y_(t-7) for a weekly pattern in daily data, removes a repeating seasonal pattern.

Difference as little as possible: take the seasonal difference first when the pattern is strong, since it may remove the trend as well; a large negative autocorrelation at lag 1, around -0.4 to -0.5 or below, is the classic sign of over-differencing.

A model of differences must be added back up to forecast the original series; the d and D in ARIMA(p, d, q)(P, D, Q)s do that automatically, which is why they're usually set in the model rather than by differencing by hand.

lessons.title: Testing for stationarity: ADF and KPSS
objectives: Run and interpret the ADF and KPSS tests
Use the two tests together and know their blind spots
key_points: The augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test's null hypothesis is a unit root, a non-stationary random-walk-like series, so a small p-value is evidence of stationarity; statsmodels' adfuller returns the statistic, the p-value and the number of lags used.

The KPSS test turns the roles round: its null is stationarity, so a small p-value is evidence against it; statsmodels' kpss only reports p-values between 0.01 and 0.1 and warns when the true one lies outside that range.

Read them together: both pointing to stationarity is good evidence; KPSS stationary but ADF not suggests a trend-stationary series, whose deterministic trend should be removed; ADF stationary but KPSS not suggests one that needs differencing.

Neither test is designed for seasonal patterns, and both lose power with structural breaks or short series; slowly decaying autocorrelation at the seasonal lags is the clearer sign that a seasonal difference is needed.
Treat the tests as a guide, not a rule: choose the simplest differencing that leaves residual autocorrelation looking like noise, and confirm the choice by comparing forecasts in a backtest.

lessons.title: Autocorrelation: ACF, PACF and white noise
objectives: Read ACF and PACF plots
Use them to suggest AR, MA and seasonal terms
Test whether what's left is white noise
key_points: The autocorrelation function (ACF) gives the correlation between a series and itself k periods earlier; the partial autocorrelation (PACF) gives that correlation after removing the effect of the lags in between.

A seasonal series has ACF spikes at multiples of its period, such as lags 7, 14 and 21 for a weekly pattern; spikes that die away very slowly mean the series needs seasonal differencing before any ARMA terms are chosen.

On a stationary series, an ACF that cuts off after lag q while the PACF tails off suggests MA(q), and a PACF that cuts off after lag p while the ACF tails off suggests AR(p); read the seasonal lags the same way for seasonal terms.

After a weekly difference, a single negative ACF spike at lag 7, with little at 14 or 21 and a PACF that tails off at 7, 14 and 21, is the classic signature of a seasonal MA(1) term, written (0, 1, 1) with period 7.

White noise has no autocorrelation, and about 95% of its sample autocorrelations fall within ±1.96/√n; the Ljung-Box test checks many lags at once, and a small p-value means there's still structure for a model to capture.

"""Lab 2: test which transformation makes the series stationary, and read its autocorrelation."""

import warnings

import numpy as np
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf, adfuller, kpss, pacf

from ts_common import clean_series, load

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")          # kpss warns when its p-value is beyond its table (below 0.01 or above 0.1)

ly = np.log(clean_series(load()))
versions = {
    "log": ly,
    "first difference": ly.diff(),
    "weekly difference": ly.diff(7),
    "weekly then first difference": ly.diff(7).diff(),
}
print(f"{'series':30} {'ADF p':>8} {'KPSS p':>8}")
for name, s in versions.items():
    s = s.dropna()
    # TODO 1: the ADF test's p-value (null: a unit root) and the KPSS test's (null: stationary)
    adf_p = kpss_p = float("nan")
    print(f"{name:30} {adf_p:8.4f} {kpss_p:8.4f}")

# The autocorrelation at lags 1, 7 and 14, and the partial autocorrelation of the weekly difference
for name in ["log", "weekly difference", "weekly then first difference"]:
    r = acf(versions[name].dropna(), nlags=14)
    print(f"ACF of {name}: lag 1 {r[1]:.3f}, lag 7 {r[7]:.3f}, lag 14 {r[14]:.3f}")
p = pacf(versions["weekly difference"].dropna(), nlags=14)
print(f"PACF of weekly difference: lag 1 {p[1]:.3f}, lag 2 {p[2]:.3f}, lag 7 {p[7]:.3f}, lag 14 {p[14]:.3f}")

# TODO 2: is the weekly difference white noise? A Ljung-Box test over 14 lags
print("Ljung-Box on the weekly difference, 14 lags: not done yet")

hints: adfuller and kpss both return a tuple; the p-value is its second item, [1].
KPSS p-values of exactly 0.1 mean 'at least 0.1': statsmodels caps them and warns (the script hides the warning).
The ADF test on log demand gives 0.0667, not significant at 5%, while KPSS doesn't reject stationarity: the pattern of a trend-stationary series.

modules.title: Exponential smoothing and ARIMA
modules.summary: Fit the two classical families of forecasting models with statsmodels: exponential smoothing (ETS), and SARIMA with regressors for holidays and campaigns, chosen by AIC and checked through their residuals.

lessons.title: Exponential smoothing and ETS models
objectives: Explain simple, Holt and Holt-Winters exponential smoothing
Fit an ETS model in statsmodels and read its parameters
Choose additive, multiplicative and damped components
key_points: Simple exponential smoothing forecasts with a weighted average of past values whose weights shrink geometrically: the level updates as l_t = αy_t + (1 - α)l_(t-1), so α near 1 follows recent values and a small α averages a long history.
Holt's method adds a trend updated with its own smoothing parameter β, and Holt-Winters adds a seasonal component updated with γ; a γ near 0 means the seasonal pattern is treated as fixed.

ETS models (error, trend, seasonal) put these methods on a statistical footing with additive or multiplicative errors, which gives a likelihood for comparing models by AIC, and prediction intervals; statsmodels has ETSModel.
A damped trend multiplies the trend by φ, between 0 and 1, at every step ahead, so long-range forecasts level off instead of extending a trend for ever; statsmodels bounds φ below at 0.8 by default.
ETS has no way to include known future events such as public holidays or campaigns, so it forecasts them as ordinary days; when they matter, use a model with regressors or adjust those days by hand.

lessons.title: ARIMA models
objectives: Explain the AR, I and MA parts of ARIMA(p, d, q)
Identify candidate orders and compare them by AIC
Check a fitted model through its residuals
key_points: ARIMA(p, d, q) models the series after d differences with p autoregressive terms (weights on its own past values) and q moving-average terms (weights on past forecast errors).

Find candidates from the ACF and PACF of the differenced series, then compare a small grid of nearby orders by AIC (Akaike information criterion), which rewards fit and penalises parameters: lower is better, and differences under about 2 are effectively ties.

AIC only compares models fitted to the same data with the same differencing, because differencing changes the series being fitted; compare models with different d or D by their errors in a backtest instead.
Check the chosen model's residuals: they should look like white noise, with no ACF spikes and a Ljung-Box p-value well above 0.05; leftover structure means the model has missed a pattern.
The differencing decides what long-range forecasts do: with d = 0 they return to the mean, with d = 1 they flatten at a level, and with d = 1 plus a constant, or d = 2, they follow a straight line.

lessons.title: SARIMA and regressors for known events
objectives: Add seasonal terms with SARIMA(p, d, q)(P, D, Q)s
Include holidays, campaigns and Fourier terms as regressors
Interpret regression coefficients on a log scale
key_points: SARIMA(p, d, q)(P, D, Q)s adds seasonal AR and MA terms at multiples of the period s, and D seasonal differences: SARIMA(1,0,0)(0,1,1)7 takes one weekly difference and has one AR term and one weekly MA term.

statsmodels' SARIMAX adds regressors (exog): the model becomes a regression with SARIMA errors, and every regressor's future values must be supplied to forecast, so use only what's known in advance, such as public holidays and planned campaigns.

Fourier terms, sine and cosine waves with periods of a year and its fractions, let a SARIMA with a weekly period follow a smooth yearly pattern too, since a seasonal period of s = 365 is impractical to estimate.
On log demand, a regressor's coefficient b multiplies demand by exp(b): a holiday coefficient of -1.33 means about 0.27 of a normal day's demand, and a campaign coefficient of 0.49 about 1.63 times.
Seasonal models need history: several full cycles to estimate seasonal terms, and enough occurrences of each event, such as several years of each public holiday, to estimate its effect.

"""Lab 3: fit exponential smoothing and SARIMA models to log demand, and compare them on the holdout."""

import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox
from statsmodels.tsa.exponential_smoothing.ets import ETSModel
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX

from ts_common import HORIZON, TEST_START, calendar, clean_series, load, scores

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

y = clean_series(load())
train, test = y[:pd.Timestamp(TEST_START) - pd.Timedelta(days=1)], y[TEST_START:]
X = calendar(y.index)
X_train, X_test = X.loc[train.index], X.loc[test.index]

snaive = np.tile(train.iloc[-7:].to_numpy(), 4)
print(f"{'seasonal naive':32} MAE {scores(test, snaive)['MAE']:6.1f}")

# ETS with additive errors, a damped additive trend and additive weekly seasonality, on log demand
ets = ETSModel(np.log(train), error="add", trend="add", damped_trend=True,
               seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=7).fit(disp=False)
ets_fc = np.exp(ets.forecast(HORIZON))
print(f"{'ETS(A,Ad,A)':32} MAE {scores(test, ets_fc)['MAE']:6.1f}  alpha {ets.smoothing_level:.3f}  "
      f"gamma {ets.smoothing_seasonal:.3f}  phi {ets.damping_trend:.3f}")

# TODO 1: compare SARIMA orders by AIC: ARMA(p, q) errors with a seasonal difference and a seasonal MA term
fits = {}
for p, q in [(1, 0)]:                       # add (0, 1), (1, 1) and (2, 1)
    fits[(p, q)] = SARIMAX(np.log(train), exog=X_train, order=(p, 0, q), seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 7)).fit(disp=False)
    print(f"SARIMA({p},0,{q})(0,1,1)7 with calendar   AIC {fits[(p, q)].aic:9.1f}")
best = min(fits, key=lambda k: fits[k].aic)
model = fits[best]
lb_p = acorr_ljungbox(model.resid[8:], lags=[14])["lb_pvalue"].iloc[0]
print(f"Best by AIC: {best}; Ljung-Box p-value of its residuals (14 lags): {lb_p:.3f}")
print(f"Holiday coefficient {model.params['holiday']:.3f} (x{np.exp(model.params['holiday']):.2f} demand); "
      f"campaign {model.params['campaign']:.3f} (x{np.exp(model.params['campaign']):.2f})")

# Forecast the holdout with the best SARIMA and score it, then the same model without the calendar
sarima_fc = np.exp(model.get_forecast(HORIZON, exog=X_test).predicted_mean)
print(f"{'SARIMA with calendar':32} MAE {scores(test, sarima_fc)['MAE']:6.1f}")
plain = SARIMAX(np.log(train), order=(best[0], 0, best[1]), seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 7)).fit(disp=False)
plain_fc = np.exp(plain.forecast(HORIZON))
print(f"{'SARIMA without calendar':32} MAE {scores(test, plain_fc)['MAE']:6.1f}")
days = test.index[test.index.isin(pd.to_datetime(["2025-12-16", "2025-12-25", "2025-12-26"]))]
print("Holidays in the holdout, actual / with calendar / without:")
for d in days:
    print(f"  {d.date()}  {test[d]:5.0f}  {sarima_fc[d]:7.1f}  {plain_fc[d]:7.1f}")

hints: SARIMAX needs exog for the forecast period as well: get_forecast(HORIZON, exog=X_test).
exp() turns forecasts of log demand back into sachets.
If a fit warns that it didn't converge, the script hides the warning; check that its AIC is close to the others'.

modules.title: Forecasting with machine learning
modules.summary: Turn a series into a supervised learning problem with lag and calendar features, forecast four weeks ahead with gradient boosting, and avoid the leaks that make such models look better than they are.

lessons.title: From a series to a table of features
objectives: Build lag, rolling and calendar features
Choose lags that respect the forecast horizon
Spot features that leak the future
key_points: Feature-based forecasting turns a series into rows: the target is the value on a day, and the features describe what was known before it, such as earlier values (lags), statistics of earlier values and calendar facts.

Every feature must exist at forecast time: to forecast up to 28 days ahead with one model, use lags of at least 28 days, such as y.shift(28), and rolling statistics of shifted values, such as y.shift(28).rolling(28).mean().

A rolling statistic that isn't shifted includes the day being predicted, and a centred window includes days after it; both leak the target and make holdout errors look better than real forecasts will be.
Calendar features (day of week, month, public holidays, planned campaigns, Fourier terms) are known for any future date and let the model learn their effects from the whole history at once.

Tree models can't predict beyond the range of targets they were trained on, so they can't extend a trend by themselves; model the target relative to a recent level, such as log(y / rolling mean), and convert back after predicting.

lessons.title: Gradient boosting forecasters: direct and recursive strategies
objectives: Fit HistGradientBoostingRegressor to lag and calendar features
Compare direct and recursive multi-step strategies
Produce quantile forecasts for intervals
key_points: Gradient boosting builds an ensemble of shallow trees, each fitted to the errors of those before it; scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingRegressor is fast on large tables and handles missing values without imputation.

A recursive strategy trains a one-step model and feeds each forecast back in as the next step's lag, so errors compound over the horizon; a direct strategy trains a model per horizon, or one model whose lags are all at least the horizon, so no forecast is reused.

One model can learn from many related series at once, such as every clinic's demand with a clinic feature, which helps series with short histories; classical models such as ARIMA are usually fitted to one series at a time.

loss='quantile' with quantile=0.1 and quantile=0.9 trains models for the 10th and 90th percentiles, an 80% interval; check how often held-out values fall inside it, because quantile models can be badly calibrated, especially on rare days such as holidays.

Machine learning forecasters shine with many related series, rich known-in-advance features or non-linear effects; on one regular series a well-specified SARIMA or ETS model is often as accurate, and easier to explain.

"""Lab 4: forecast four weeks ahead with gradient boosting on lag and calendar features."""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor

from ts_common import HORIZON, TEST_START, calendar, clean_series, load, scores


def features(y):
    """One row per day, using only values at least 28 days old, so one model can forecast 1 to 28 days ahead."""
    X = calendar(y.index)
    X["dayofweek"] = y.index.dayofweek
    X["month"] = y.index.month
    X["lag28"] = y.shift(28)
    # TODO 1: a 35-day lag, and the same weekday 52 weeks earlier (lag 364)
    # the mean of the 28 days that end 28 days before the day being forecast
    X["mean28"] = y.shift(28).rolling(28).mean()
    return X


def main():
    y = clean_series(load())
    X = features(y)
    target = np.log(y / X["mean28"])                 # demand relative to its recent level, so trees needn't extrapolate
    ok = X.notna().all(axis=1)
    cut = pd.Timestamp(TEST_START)
    train_rows, test_rows = ok & (X.index < cut), X.index >= cut
    print(f"Training rows: {train_rows.sum()} from {X.index[train_rows][0].date()}; test rows: {test_rows.sum()}")

    # TODO 2: fit HistGradientBoostingRegressor on the training rows, forecast the test rows, and score it
    model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=300, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=0)
    model.fit(X[train_rows], target[train_rows])
    forecast = X.loc[test_rows, "mean28"]           # replace: mean28 times exp(the model's prediction)
    s = scores(y[test_rows], forecast)
    print(f"Gradient boosting, direct 1-28 days: MAE {s['MAE']:.1f}  RMSE {s['RMSE']:.1f}")

    # The leak: a 7-day rolling mean that forgets to shift, so it includes the day being predicted
    leaky = X.assign(mean7=y.rolling(7).mean())
    model_leak = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=300, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=0)
    model_leak.fit(leaky[train_rows], target[train_rows])
    leak_fc = leaky.loc[test_rows, "mean28"] * np.exp(model_leak.predict(leaky[test_rows]))
    print(f"With an unshifted 7-day mean (a leak): MAE {scores(y[test_rows], leak_fc)['MAE']:.1f}")

    # TODO 3: 10% and 90% quantile models for an 80% interval, and how often the holdout falls inside it
    bounds = {}
    for q in (0.1, 0.9):
        m = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=300, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=0)   # make it a quantile model
        m.fit(X[train_rows], target[train_rows])
        bounds[q] = X.loc[test_rows, "mean28"] * np.exp(m.predict(X[test_rows]))
    inside = ((y[test_rows] >= bounds[0.1]) & (y[test_rows] <= bounds[0.9])).mean()
    print(f"80% interval: covers {inside:.3f} of the holdout, mean width {np.mean(bounds[0.9] - bounds[0.1]):.1f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: X.notna().all(axis=1) keeps only rows where every feature exists; lag364 needs a year of history.
A leak doesn't always look dramatic: a plausible small improvement is exactly why it goes unnoticed.
Keep main() guarded by if __name__ == '__main__': lab 5 imports features() from this file.

modules.title: Backtesting, metrics and prediction intervals
modules.summary: Evaluate forecasters the way they'll be used: backtests from several origins, metrics chosen for the decision, and prediction intervals whose coverage is checked.

lessons.title: Backtesting with rolling origins
objectives: Run a rolling-origin backtest with TimeSeriesSplit
Choose the number of folds, the test size and the gap
Keep tuning and feature choices out of the test folds
key_points: A backtest (time series cross-validation) repeats the holdout from several forecast origins: fit on the data up to each origin, forecast the next horizon, and pool the errors, which gives a steadier estimate than one test period.

TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=6, test_size=28) gives six consecutive 28-day test windows at the end of the data, each after an expanding training window; max_train_size makes the window slide instead, and gap leaves days out between training and test.
Refit the model at every origin, as it would be refitted in production, and use only information available at that origin, including for filling gaps, transforming the series and building features.

Tune hyperparameters and model orders on earlier folds or inside each training window, and keep the final folds for the comparison; picking a model because it won on the very folds you report gives an optimistic score.

Look at errors by horizon and by period, not only overall: errors usually grow with the horizon, and a model that wins on average can still fail on the days that matter, such as holidays or the season's peak.

lessons.title: Forecast accuracy metrics, and the traps in MAPE
objectives: Compute MAE, RMSE, MAPE, WAPE and MASE
Choose a metric that fits the decision
Recognise when MAPE misleads
key_points: MAE, the mean absolute error, is in the series' units and is smallest for a forecast of the median; RMSE, the root mean squared error, is smallest for the mean and punishes large errors, such as a missed holiday, much more.

MAPE, the mean absolute percentage error, divides each error by the actual value, so it's infinite or undefined when an actual is zero and explodes when actuals are small, letting a few quiet days dominate the average.

MAPE caps the cost of forecasting too low at 100% but not the cost of forecasting too high, so choosing forecasts by MAPE favours ones that run low: for an actual of 100, forecasting 0 costs 100% while forecasting 250 costs 150%.

WAPE, the sum of absolute errors divided by the sum of actuals, weights days by volume and copes with zeros; MASE divides the MAE by the in-sample MAE of a seasonal naive forecast, so below 1 beats that baseline and series of different sizes compare fairly.

Choose the metric from the decision: running out of stock on busy days calls for errors in units, such as MAE or WAPE, and when under- and over-forecasting cost different amounts, a weighted or quantile loss fits better than any symmetric metric.

lessons.title: Prediction intervals and coverage
objectives: Explain what a prediction interval promises
Get intervals from models, quantile regression and past errors
Check an interval's coverage in a backtest
key_points: A prediction interval gives a range that should contain a future value with a stated probability, such as 80%; it's wider than a confidence interval for a mean, because it includes the noise in a single future value.

Model-based intervals, such as SARIMAX's get_forecast(...).conf_int(alpha=0.2) or ETS's, assume the model is right and its errors are well behaved; they widen with the horizon but miss uncertainty from choosing the model and from unusual events.

Empirical intervals take quantiles of past forecast errors, such as the 10th and 90th percentiles of log(actual / forecast) from earlier backtest folds, and apply them to new forecasts; they work with any model, including gradient boosting.

Check coverage: in a backtest, an 80% interval should contain about 80% of actual values; far less means it's too narrow, far more means it's wider than it needs to be, and coverage is worth checking by horizon and by season too.

Use intervals for decisions: stocking to the 90th percentile of total demand over the lead time runs out about one period in ten if that percentile is well calibrated, so the service level a store chooses sets the quantile to plan for.

"""Lab 5: backtest four forecasters from six origins, compare metrics, and check prediction intervals."""

import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit
from statsmodels.tsa.exponential_smoothing.ets import ETSModel
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX

from lab4_boosting import features
from ts_common import HORIZON, calendar, clean_series, load, scores

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
y = clean_series(load())
X = calendar(y.index)
F = features(y)
gb_target = np.log(y / F["mean28"])
rows = []                                            # one row per model, day and fold
gb_errors = []                                       # log(actual / forecast) from earlier folds

# Six folds, each testing the 28 days after its origin and training on everything before it
splits = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=6, test_size=HORIZON)
for fold, (tr, te) in enumerate(splits.split(y), 1):
    train, test = y.iloc[tr], y.iloc[te]
    fc = {"seasonal naive": np.tile(train.iloc[-7:].to_numpy(), 4)}
    ets = ETSModel(np.log(train), error="add", trend="add", damped_trend=True, seasonal="add",
                   seasonal_periods=7).fit(disp=False)
    fc["ETS"] = np.exp(ets.forecast(HORIZON)).to_numpy()
    sar = SARIMAX(np.log(train), exog=X.iloc[tr], order=(1, 0, 0), seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 7)).fit(disp=False)
    pred = sar.get_forecast(HORIZON, exog=X.iloc[te])
    fc["SARIMA"] = np.exp(pred.predicted_mean).to_numpy()
    # TODO 1: SARIMA's 80% prediction interval, from conf_int(alpha=0.2), back on the original scale
    sar_lo = sar_hi = fc["SARIMA"]
    ok = F.iloc[tr].notna().all(axis=1).to_numpy()
    gb = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=300, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=0)
    gb.fit(F.iloc[tr][ok], gb_target.iloc[tr][ok])
    fc["gradient boosting"] = (F.iloc[te]["mean28"] * np.exp(gb.predict(F.iloc[te]))).to_numpy()
    # TODO 2: an empirical 80% interval from the 10th and 90th percentiles of earlier folds' errors
    if gb_errors:
        lo, hi = 0.0, 0.0
        emp_lo, emp_hi = fc["gradient boosting"] * np.exp(lo), fc["gradient boosting"] * np.exp(hi)
    else:
        emp_lo = emp_hi = np.full(HORIZON, np.nan)
    gb_errors.append(np.log(test.to_numpy() / fc["gradient boosting"]))
    for name, f in fc.items():
        rows.append(pd.DataFrame({"model": name, "fold": fold, "date": test.index, "h": np.arange(1, HORIZON + 1),
                                  "actual": test.to_numpy(), "forecast": f,
                                  "sar_lo": sar_lo, "sar_hi": sar_hi, "emp_lo": emp_lo, "emp_hi": emp_hi}))
    print(f"Fold {fold}: origin {train.index[-1].date()}, tests {test.index[0].date()} to {test.index[-1].date()}")

bt = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
first_train = y.iloc[:len(y) - 6 * HORIZON]

# Every metric for every model over all 168 backtest days
print(f"\n{'model':18} {'MAE':>7} {'RMSE':>7} {'MAPE':>7} {'WAPE':>7} {'MASE':>7}")
for name, g in bt.groupby("model", sort=False):
    s = scores(g["actual"], g["forecast"], first_train)
    print(f"{name:18} {s['MAE']:7.1f} {s['RMSE']:7.1f} {s['MAPE']:7.1f} {s['WAPE']:7.1f} {s['MASE']:7.3f}")

sar = bt[bt["model"] == "SARIMA"].copy()
by_week = sar.groupby((sar["h"] - 1) // 7 + 1).apply(lambda g: np.mean(np.abs(g.actual - g.forecast)))
print("\nSARIMA MAE by week of the horizon:", by_week.round(1).tolist())

# MAPE's traps on a small-count series: amoxicillin, forecast with the mean of each weekday over the last 4 weeks
amox = clean_series(load(), "amoxicillin_courses")
parts = []
for tr, te in splits.split(amox):
    recent = amox.iloc[tr].iloc[-28:]
    profile = recent.groupby(recent.index.dayofweek).mean()
    parts.append(pd.DataFrame({"actual": amox.iloc[te].to_numpy(),
                               "forecast": profile.reindex(amox.index[te].dayofweek).to_numpy()}))
am = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)
nonzero = am["actual"] > 0
print(f"\nAmoxicillin: {int((~nonzero).sum())} of {len(am)} backtest days are zero")
for k in (1.0, 0.8):
    s, s_nz = scores(am["actual"], k * am["forecast"]), scores(am["actual"][nonzero], k * am["forecast"][nonzero])
    print(f"Forecast x{k}: MAE {s['MAE']:.2f}, WAPE {s['WAPE']:.1f}, MAPE {s['MAPE']}, MAPE on non-zero days {s_nz['MAPE']:.1f}")

cover = ((sar["actual"] >= sar["sar_lo"]) & (sar["actual"] <= sar["sar_hi"])).mean()
print(f"\nSARIMA 80% intervals: coverage {cover:.3f}, mean width {np.mean(sar['sar_hi'] - sar['sar_lo']):.1f}")
gbe = bt[(bt["model"] == "gradient boosting") & bt["emp_lo"].notna()]
cover = ((gbe["actual"] >= gbe["emp_lo"]) & (gbe["actual"] <= gbe["emp_hi"])).mean()
print(f"Gradient boosting, empirical 80% intervals (folds 2-6): coverage {cover:.3f}, "
      f"mean width {np.mean(gbe['emp_hi'] - gbe['emp_lo']):.1f}")

hints: conf_int() returns a DataFrame with a lower and an upper column; .to_numpy().T splits it into two arrays.
Fold 1 has no earlier errors to calibrate an empirical interval, so its coverage is measured on folds 2 to 6.
MASE uses the in-sample MAE of a weekly seasonal naive forecast on the data before the first origin.

project.title: Four-week medicine forecasts for the district store
project.brief: The district medical store orders oral rehydration salts, paracetamol and amoxicillin every four weeks, and wants forecasts it can trust for 1 to 28 January 2026. Using demand.csv, forecast all three medicines daily with 80% prediction intervals, backed by a backtest from at least six origins. The series differ: ORS has a strong rainy-season peak and campaign spikes, paracetamol peaks in the cold season, and amoxicillin is small counts with some zero days, so a metric or method that suits one may not suit another. Choose a method per medicine with reasons, check its residuals and its interval coverage, and give the store a 28-day total for each medicine with an upper planning figure. Finish with a one-page note for the store manager.
deliverables: A backtest of at least three methods per medicine, including seasonal naive, from at least six origins, with MAE, WAPE and MASE (and MAPE only where it's defined and meaningful)
Your chosen method for each medicine, with the reason and its residual checks
Daily forecasts for 1 to 28 January 2026 with 80% prediction intervals, and those intervals' coverage in your backtest
A 28-day total for each medicine with an upper planning figure, such as its 90th percentile, and how you worked it out
A one-page note for the store manager: the forecasts, how far to trust them, and what would change them, such as a campaign added to the plan

rubric.name: Backtest design
rubric.description: Rolling origins with refits, no information from after each origin, the same folds for every method, and errors examined by horizon.

rubric.name: Model choice and diagnostics
rubric.description: Methods suit each series, orders or settings are justified, and residuals are checked for leftover structure.

rubric.name: Metrics fit for purpose
rubric.description: Metrics match the ordering decision, MAPE is avoided or handled where actuals are small or zero, and MASE compares series fairly.

rubric.name: Intervals and coverage
rubric.description: 80% intervals are produced for every day, their backtest coverage is reported, and they're adjusted when coverage is far from 80%.

rubric.name: Forecasts and planning figures
rubric.description: January forecasts handle the 1 January holiday, and the 28-day totals and upper figures are computed correctly, not by adding daily percentiles.

rubric.name: Communication
rubric.description: The note is clear to a store manager, honest about uncertainty and specific about what would change the forecasts.

project.submit: Paste your code (or a link to your notebook), the backtest tables, the January forecasts with intervals, the 28-day totals and the note.
